title: Observability — Kernel Forensics (dmesg + ZFS dbgmsg, fingerprinted)
description: Kernel ring buffer as a first-class signal — not a place you only look after something is on fire. Shows severity shape, subsystem chatter, critical-event fingerprints, and overlays kernel errors as annotations on every other dashboard via a Loki annotation query. Splunk indexes dmesg too, but it cannot annotate latency panels with kernel events in real time without expensive per-dashboard scripting.

panels.title: Headline — the bad stuff (count today, kept zero = good)
Errors/sec (last 5m, level ≥ err)
panels.description: Rate of kernel messages at severity err or worse. Steady state should be near 0. Sustained > 1/sec means investigate.

panels.title: OOM kills (24h)
panels.description: `Out of memory: Killed process` matches. Each one is a real signal — a process the kernel decided to murder because the system was under memory pressure. Splunk would count these too, but you'd have to write the SPL.

panels.title: Machine Checks (24h)
panels.description: MCE / Machine check exceptions — hardware-level errors (ECC, cache parity, CPU thermal). Any non-zero count is investigate-now territory. Splunk can match the regex but won't tell you it's hardware.

panels.title: Soft lockups + RCU stalls (24h)
panels.description: `soft lockup` = a CPU stuck in a loop without scheduling. `rcu: INFO: rcu_sched stall` = RCU couldn't make forward progress. Both mean *something held a CPU for too long* — usually a driver or filesystem under stress. Useful to correlate with latency-spike annotations.

panels.title: ZFS events (24h)
panels.description: All ZFS dbgmsg + ZED-emitted events. Most are info-level (scrub start/end, snapshot taken). Spikes here cross-referenced with bio_latency = ZFS doing real work. ZFS-on-Linux's diagnostic chatter is unique to this stack — Splunk can index it but won't have ZFS-aware dashboards built in.

panels.title: Kernel panics (24h)
panels.description: Should be 0 forever. Panics by definition don't get to log themselves cleanly — but the boot AFTER a panic logs a panic-was-detected message via the kernel's pstore + kdump path. Anything other than 0 is a real incident.

panels.title: Kernel messages/sec by severity (stacked)
panels.description: The shape of kernel chatter. Healthy systems are mostly info/notice. Sudden walls of warn/err = something just broke. Compare against the same window on bio_latency / process exec rate dashboards via the kernel-error annotations.

panels.title: ZFS dbgmsg rate (zfs-dbgmsg job)
panels.description: Rate of messages on the ZFS debug ring buffer. Scrubs / resilvers / TRIM / dedup ops all generate dbgmsg activity. A flat-line followed by a sudden burst = ZFS just kicked off something heavy. Pair with bio_latency heatmap to see the actual disk impact.

panels.title: Critical kernel events (sorted newest first)
panels.description: The actual lines that triggered the headline counters. Time-aligned with the severity-rate chart above. Click into a line to see the surrounding context.

panels.title: Rate by syslog identifier (top 10)
panels.description: Which kernel subsystems are producing the most messages right now. `kernel` (catch-all) plus any kthreads that set their own syslog id (zed, libvirtd-helpers, etc.). Outliers here = something noisy.

panels.title: Rate by subsystem prefix (extracted from message)
panels.description: Many kernel subsystems prefix their messages — `BTRFS:`, `EXT4-fs`, `zfs:`, `audit:`, `nf_conntrack:`. Extracted via regex so you can see which kernel-side feature is chatty even when syslog_id is just `kernel`. The killer view for ZFS perf debugging on a noisy box.

panels.title: Live tail — recent kernel + ZFS dbgmsg stream (warn+)

options.content:
### Why this dashboard exists

Most ops teams treat `dmesg` like a fire extinguisher — you only reach for it when something's already burning. That's backwards. The kernel ring buffer is **the most authoritative signal source on the entire system** — it's written by the code that's closest to the hardware, the storage, the network, the scheduler. Visualizing it first-class is one of the highest-ROI things you can do for a platform.

### What this gives you that Splunk doesn't

1. **Annotations on every other dashboard.** The `Kernel errors` annotation on this dashboard is configured globally — paste the same `annotations` block into any other dashboard and you get red vertical markers on every panel that line up with `dmesg` errors. Splunk has annotation support but it's per-dashboard, manual, and brittle.
2. **ZFS dbgmsg as a first-class stream.** `/proc/spl/kstat/zfs/dbgmsg` is a ZFS-only diagnostic ring buffer; the `zfs-dbgmsg` Promtail job ships it to Loki. No Splunk app does this; you'd write a forwarder.
3. **Subsystem extraction by regex over the live stream.** The `regexp` operator extracts the `BTRFS:` / `EXT4-fs` / `zfs:` prefix and lets you `topk(10)` who's chatty. Splunk can do this at query time but the SPL is ugly and slow on big indexes.
4. **Sub-second-resolution rates.** Loki tracks ingest time at nanosecond granularity; we display per-second rates. Splunk's default time bucketing is minute-resolution; sub-second forensics requires `bin span=1s` and gets expensive.

### Pair this dashboard with

- **eBPF Deep Dive** (`/d/kldload-ebpf-deep`) — when the annotations on a Tetragon event-rate spike line up with kernel errors here, you know which kernel subsystem caused the spike.
- **Block I/O Latency** (`/d/kldload-block-io-latency`) — `bio_latency_seconds_bucket` heatmaps with kernel-error annotations overlaid = the canonical 'why was the disk slow at 1am' view.
- **Tetragon eBPF Security** (`/d/kldload-tetragon`) — process events on the same time axis as kernel events. OOM kill → see the process that got killed → see what it was doing right before it died.

### How to extend

- Add an annotation block like the one in this dashboard's JSON to other dashboards — same query, instant correlation.
- Add ZFS-specific fingerprints (scrub start, resilver, TRIM, vdev fault) as named counters.
- Run `bcc-tools` (when we add them to the host in #30) and pipe their output to journal with `systemd-cat -p info` — they become dashboard-visible automatically.
